name: Communication Snapshot
semantics: Defines what the Communication Snapshot asks. Two vocabulary estimates (integers, bucketed in the UI; vocab_understands may also be the string ‘unsure’, which never matches any rule) and 16 behavior items. Behavior values are yes | sometimes | not_yet, except parent_hearing_concern and lost_skills, which are yes | no, and understood_by_others, which is most | about_half | less_than_half (mirroring the Milestone Navigator’s clarity answers). Optional per-item ‘recap’ and per-bucket ‘phrase’ strings are display-only: they make the recap and the printed visit notes read as sentences and are never evaluated. ‘sometimes’ is a real developmental answer and never counts as absence. Items carry asked_from_months and optional asked_until_months; the UI hides items outside the child’s (corrected) age window. Every behavior id referenced by floors.v1.json or interpretation.v1.json must exist here (the floors grader checks referential integrity). No word checklist ships in v1: parents estimate counts directly, which keeps the instrument clear of the CDI item-overlap question entirely (see cdi_exclusion/README.md, which remains the contract for any future checklist version).

corrected_age.note: If your child was born more than 3 weeks early and is under 24 months, we use their corrected age (age counted from the due date). This is the standard way to look at development for children born early.

vocab_says.prompt: About how many words does your child say?
vocab_says.help: Count any word your child uses on purpose to mean something, in any language your family speaks. Word approximations count if they are used consistently, like ‘baba’ for bottle. Animal sounds used to name the animal count (‘moo’ for cow). Leave out ‘mama’ and ‘dada’: they usually come first, and the CDC milestones count the words beyond them. Do not count sounds that don’t stand for anything yet.

buckets.label: 200 or more, or too many to count

vocab_says.bucket_note: Bucket boundaries are aligned to every threshold the interpretation rules use (0, 1, 3, 10, 50), so a bucket can never straddle a line. The old ‘1 to 5’ bucket was split at 3 on 2026-11-02 because CDC’s 18-month milestone is three or more words besides mama or dada.

vocab_understands.prompt: About how many words does your child understand?
vocab_understands.help: Words your child responds to even if they can’t say them, like looking at the dog when you say ‘dog’, or getting excited for ‘bath’. Count across every language your family speaks. A rough guess is fine; most children understand far more than they say. Not sure? Name a familiar thing, like ‘ball’ or ‘shoe’, without pointing, and watch whether they look at it or go get it.
vocab_understands.bucket_note: Bucket boundaries align to the threshold the rules use (10). ‘I’m not sure’ is stored as the string ‘unsure’, which never matches a rule (the engine’s isNaN guard), and it is printed on the visit notes as not sure. Before 2026-11-02 the lowest bucket was ‘Only a few, or not sure’, which merged a red-flag answer with uncertainty.

behaviors.help: When you say their name from behind or beside them, without touching them, do they look or turn toward you most of the time?
Strings of sounds like ‘ba-ba’, ‘da-da’, ‘ma-ma’, not just cooing vowel sounds.
You make a sound or say something, they respond, you respond back. The exchange can be sounds, smiles, or words; what matters is the back-and-forth.

behaviors.prompt: Tries to copy sounds or words
behaviors.help: Attempts count, even if the copy is not close. What matters is that they try.

behaviors.prompt: Looks at your face to share enjoyment
behaviors.help: When something is funny or exciting, do they look at you as if to say ‘did you see that?’
Waving bye-bye, reaching arms up to be picked up, shaking their head, pushing things away to mean ‘no’.
Points at something they want, like a snack or a toy out of reach.

behaviors.prompt: Points to show you something interesting
behaviors.help: This is different from pointing to ask. Here the point means ‘look at that!’, just to share it with you, like pointing at a dog or a plane.
When you point at something across the room, do they look at the thing you’re pointing at, not just at your finger?
Something like ‘bring me the ball’ or ‘sit down’, said in words alone, without you pointing or gesturing at the same time.
Their own combinations, like ‘more milk’ or ‘daddy go’. Memorized chunks used as one unit, like ‘all done’ or ‘thank you’, do not count here.

behaviors.prompt: Puts two or more words together with an action word
behaviors.help: Phrases where one word says what is happening, like ‘doggie run’, ‘mama go’, or ‘eat cookie’. Their own phrases count; memorized chunks do not.
Talking about themselves or the family, like ‘me do it’, ‘I want juice’, or ‘we go park’. Using their own name instead most of the time counts as not yet.
You say something, they answer in words, you reply, and they answer again on the same topic: at least two back-and-forth exchanges.

behaviors.prompt: How much of your child’s speech can an unfamiliar adult understand?
behaviors.help: Not you, someone who doesn’t know your child, like a new babysitter or a stranger at the park. You will understand far more than they do; that’s normal.
behaviors.recap: How much an unfamiliar adult understands

behaviors.prompt: Do you have a feeling that your child doesn’t hear well?
behaviors.help: Any nagging sense counts: needing to be very loud, no reaction to sounds that should register, or just something you can’t quite name.
behaviors.recap: A feeling that they don’t hear well

behaviors.prompt: Has your child lost words or skills they used to have?
behaviors.recap: Lost words or skills they used to have
behaviors.help: For example, they used to say words and stopped, or used to wave or respond to their name and no longer do. Any real loss counts, at any age.
